opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's a slightly tongue-in-cheek point, but there's something real behind it. When the task is ambiguous, meaning I haven't fully specified what I want and maybe don't fully know yet myself, the "smarter" models tend to resolve that ambiguity on their own. They make a dozen assumptions about what I *must* have meant, then confidently produce several hundred lines of polished code built on those assumptions. And because it looks so good, I'm tempted to accept it.

The problem is that these systems don't actually know what I intend. They're doing a very sophisticated kind of approximate retrieval, filling the gaps with whatever is most plausible given their training distribution. "Most plausible on the web" is not the same as "what this particular user needs." So the more capable the model is at generating fluent, complete-looking artifacts, the more work I have to do afterward to figure out where it quietly went off the rails. The verification burden shifts back onto me, and it's harder because the errors are buried under competence.

A less capable model does less on its own initiative. It gives me a smaller, rougher piece, which forces me to stay in the loop and make the design decisions myself. In an ambiguous setting that's what I want, because the ambiguity is precisely the part that requires *my* judgment. The model is a useful idea generator, but I'm the one who has to be the critic.

So it's really the same argument I make about LLM-Modulo frameworks in general: these models are great at generating candidates, but correctness and intent have to come from somewhere else, whether that's an external verifier or the human. When the specification is fuzzy, the human is the verifier. A model that's too eager to be helpful can make that role harder, not easier. Sometimes a bit of dumbness is a feature, because it keeps you honest about who's actually doing the thinking.

r001.rationale: The response says a less capable model keeps the user involved in design decisions, but does not explain the preference as a didactic exchange enabled by correcting the model’s misunderstandings.

r002.rationale: It discusses ambiguity and the model making assumptions, but does not suggest clarifying the task at the outset or compare that with O1 enumerating possible approaches.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it's a little counterintuitive, I know. But think about what an ambiguous task actually is. If I give you a half-baked specification, there are many programs that are consistent with it, and I haven't yet decided which one I want. The thing I need from the model at that point is not a confident, polished answer. I need friction.

What happens with the very large models is they're extremely good at what I'd call plausible completion. They read my vague prompt, they silently resolve all the ambiguity in whatever direction the training distribution suggests, and they hand me three hundred lines of beautifully formatted code. And the code looks right. That's the problem. It looks so right that I stop thinking. I'm now in the business of verifying their interpretation instead of forming my own, and verification of someone else's guess is actually harder than specifying what you wanted in the first place. People sometimes forget that the hard part of programming was never typing.

A dumber model does something more useful for me in that situation. It gives me something slightly wrong, or incomplete, or it asks a question, or it makes a bad assumption that is obviously bad. And that mismatch is informative. It surfaces the ambiguity. I look at it and say, no, that's not what I meant, and in saying that I've just discovered what I did mean. The weak model is essentially acting as a sounding board rather than an oracle. It's closer to rubber duck debugging than to delegation.

There's also a point here about what I've called the Hans the Horse problem, where you end up unconsciously steering the system and then crediting it for being clever. With a very fluent model, I get seduced into that. With a less fluent one, the division of labor is honest: it's clear that I'm doing the thinking, and the model is doing the typing and the retrieval. For an ambiguous task, I actually want that division. Once I've converged on what the specification is, fine, then give me the strongest model you have and let it generate the boring parts. But generation and specification are different activities, and the mistake people make is reaching for the most capable generator when what they really have is a specification problem.

r001.rationale: The response says the weaker model’s obvious mistakes surface ambiguity; correcting them helps the speaker discover what they meant.

r002.rationale: It says clearer specification should come before code generation, but does not suggest doing that instead of having O1 enumerate possible approaches.

astra-6.text:
Because a smarter model may be very good at guessing what I meant—and that can hide the fact that I haven’t actually specified what I want. With an ambiguous programming task, there are several plausible things it could implement. If it picks one and produces convincing code, I may not notice the assumptions it made.

A dumber model can force me to make those assumptions explicit. I have to clarify the task, and in doing that I sometimes discover that I didn’t know exactly what I wanted either. That’s useful! The goal isn’t merely to get code quickly; it’s to get code for the problem I actually intended to solve. Ideally, of course, I want a smart model that knows when to ask a question instead of silently filling in the gaps.

r001.rationale: The response says a less capable model can force the user to clarify assumptions, but it does not explain the preference as a didactic exchange in which the user corrects the model’s misunderstandings.

r002.rationale: The response values clarifying the task, but it does not compare doing so at the outset with having O1 enumerate possible approaches.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, because if the task is ambiguous, I want the system to ask me what I mean. A more capable language model can be very good at coming up with a plausible interpretation and then writing a lot of perfectly reasonable code for that interpretation. But that may not be what I wanted at all.

A dumber model might stumble and ask a question, and that question gives me an opportunity to clarify the specification. So the issue isn't whether it can write the code. It's whether it recognizes when it doesn't yet know what code it should be writing. Being better at guessing can actually hide that problem.

r001.rationale: The response says a less capable model may ask what the user means, allowing the user to clarify the specification. It does not clearly describe correcting the model’s misunderstandings as the reason for the preference.

r002.rationale: The response does not suggest clarifying the task at the outset or compare that with having O1 enumerate possible approaches.
